## 87. The royal year: a family that spoke to nobody, and a branch ladder that poisoned its own tail

Section 47 put a crown on the hero's head: it wired the seat, the house and the
three tokens a monarch's titles need, and it left the twelve tables the royal
family actually speaks through to the generic renderer. The generic renderer
applies Karma, Discipline, Happiness, Intelligence and Appearance -- the five
impacts of `pointsForImpact`'s jump table -- and nothing else, so a reign in the
port was a random walk of unrelated events with no regard, no tabloids and no
subjects. This section wires the family: eleven more tables, a regard of its own,
and a year that is one card about one person.

Four bugs justify it. The branch ladder was written as a chain of `if (roll < X)`
tests with **no lower bound**, so a branch whose pool had no eligible row fell
through to a *later* test that also matched: the first probe showed 586
beheadings against a five percent window, one monarch in four ending a subject.
`<newspaper>`, `<castle>`, `<country-adjectival>` and `<country-possessive>`
never reached `heroToken` at all, because `resolve` only forwards a token that
starts with `hero-` or stands in an explicit list -- 876 leaked occurrences.
`<hero-royal-name>` had no case anywhere. And the two commoner pools resolved
their feedback snippet before the scenario, so the `<rb>` the feedback points at
had nothing to point at.

### 87.1 The family

Twelve tables, 580 rows, of which section 47 had wired exactly one:

| table | rows | what it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `a16_royal-house-names-enc` | 159 | Name, Estate, Palace, Castle, Country Code, Commonness Score (wired by 47) |
| `a16_royal-celebrity-interaction-scenarios-enc` | 59 | List Item, Scenario, Past/Present Tense Snippet, enjoyment and respect |
| `a16_royal-school-negative-scenarios-enc` | 54 | Teacher, Classmate, Scenario, Feedback/Log Version Snippet |
| `a16_royal-punishments-enc` | 44 | Snippet, UK/Japan/Arab Only |
| `a16_royal-tabloid-scenarios-enc` | 38 | Scenario, Log Version, regard band, age band, seat and country gates |
| `a16_royal-school-positive-scenarios-enc` | 37 | as the negative pool |
| `a16_royal-rewards-enc` | 37 | Snippet, UK/Japan/Arab Only |
| `a16_royal-commoner-negative-scenarios-enc` | 34 | Scenario, Feedback/Log Version Snippet, regard band, seat flags |
| `a16_royal-executions-enc` | 33 | Method, Scenario, Log Version, Hero Scenario, Death Snippet, Pain Score |
| `a16_royal-public-disservice-scenarios-enc` | 29 | Scenario, Log Version, Public Outrage Snippet, Respect Impact (-4/-5) |
| `a16_royal-public-service-scenarios-enc` | 28 | Scenario, Log Version, Respect Impact (+3) |
| `a16_royal-commoner-positive-scenarios-enc` | 28 | as the negative pool, with a Min Respect band |

Every pool of the family gates on the same handful of columns -- `Hero Gender`,
a `Hero Min Age`/`Hero Max Age` or `Min Age`/`Max Age` window, a `Min Respect`/
`Max Respect` band, `Hero Has Lover`, `Is Highest Ranking Royal` /
`Is Not Highest Ranking Royal`, and `UK Only` / `Japan Only` / `Arab Only` --
so the port writes one `eligible` predicate and every branch draws through it.

The executions pool is two cards in one table. `Scenario` is a subject being
executed on the hero's order ("You had Kayne YBY disemboweled."); `Hero Scenario`
is the hero being executed ("You have been publicly hanged!") and `Death Snippet`
is the fragment a death line is built from. The punishments and rewards pools hold
fragments rather than sentences ("two weeks in the royal dungeon", "a stoning"), so
the port builds the sentence around them.

### 87.2 The seat

`Sim::makeRoyal` (section 47) now also draws the castle from the house table's
`Castle` column, and it draws a **rank**. Half the royals are first in line and the
rest are a rank or two below, otherwise every `Is Not Highest Ranking Royal` row in
four pools is unreachable and the family only ever speaks to an heir. The rank picks
the seat column (`Rank 1 Female`, `Rank 2 Male`, ...), and a rank whose column is
empty falls back a step.

The hero gains nine fields (include/bl/game.h):

```
std::string royalCastle;
int royalRespect = 50;      // the country's regard, 0..100
int royalYears = 0;         // how long the reign has lasted
int royalOutrages = 0;
int royalSentences = 0;     // subjects punished
int royalGifts = 0;         // subjects rewarded
int royalExecutions = 0;    // subjects executed on the hero's order
std::string royalNewspaper;
std::string royalSubject;
```

### 87.3 The year

`Sim::royalYear`, called from `ageUp` immediately after the boating line, takes the
year outright. The first version was a single roll against a chain of windows, which
is the shape every earlier family uses and which does not survive an optional
branch: when a window's pool has no eligible row the chain falls through to the
*next* test that also matches, so the year lands in a branch it was never offered.
Here the year is instead a **weighted draw over the branches that are available**:
`have(name)` asks whether the pool holds a row the hero passes, an unavailable
branch is not in the draw at all, and the weights are the old window widths.

| weight | branch | what moves |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | the tabloid | regard - 3 |
| 8 | an ungrateful subject | regard - 2, happiness - 2 |
| 8 | a loyal subject | regard + 2, happiness + 2 |
| 8 | a royal duty | the row's Respect Impact (+3) |
| 8 | a royal disgrace | the row's Respect Impact (-4/-5), outrages + 1 |
| 8 | an invitation (18+) | the row's Enjoyment Score and Respect Impact |
| 6 | at school, negative (a pupil) | regard - 2, happiness - 2 |
| 6 | at school, positive (a pupil) | regard + 2, happiness + 1 |
| 5 | an execution on the hero's order (top seat) | regard - 4, happiness - 3 |
| 7 | a subject punished (regard < 45) | regard - 2, happiness - 1 |
| 7 | a subject rewarded (regard > 55) | regard + 2, happiness + 1 |
| 18 | a quiet year at the seat | nothing |

Before the draw, one event is not a card but a consequence: a regard at or below
eight is deposed. That branch keeps a quarter chance of firing in any one year,
draws an execution method from the family's own table, builds the death line from
the `Death Snippet` ("being executed by public hanging" becomes "public hanging"),
marks the life dead and lets the driver end it. Without the chance, a country that
hated its monarch executed him in the first year it could.

The subject of the year's card is one person, drawn once, so the card and the
journal name the same man ("Kay Shift was sentenced to a stoning for
disrespecting the crown." / "I sentenced Kay Shift to a stoning."). The regard is
clamped at every write, and every card ends with the ledger line
`"The country's regard for me is N%."`, taken from the port's own counter and not
from the data, which is the family's substitute for the game's respect bar.

### 87.4 The tokens

Four tokens had no handler and three of them could not reach the one they needed.
`heroToken` gained `hero-title` (the seat, or the hero's job, or "citizen"),
`hero-royal-name` (seat + first name), `newspaper` and `castle`. The names are
built at the seat: the paper is composed from the country with five shapes
("the %s Times", "%s Daily", "the %s Herald", "the %s Gazette", "%s Post"),
because **no table in the corpus holds a newspaper name** -- 76 occurrences of
`<newspaper>` and nothing behind them, so the port invents one and says so.

`resolve`'s gate is the trap: a token reaches `heroToken` only when it starts with
`hero-`/`hero:` or stands in an explicit list, so adding a case to `heroToken` is
silent until the name is added there too. `country-adjectival`,
`country-possessive`, `newspaper` and `castle` were added to that list.

The invitation card needed the pronoun pair pointed the other way: the pool's
`<him/her>` and `<he/she>` refer to the **celebrity**, not to the hero, and with the
pair unset every celebrity was "him". The card now draws its own guest, sets
`pronounOtherSet_ = true` and `pronounOtherFemale_` from that guest's gender, and
substitutes `<celebrity>` and `<celebrity2>` before resolving -- so "Margot Robbie
asks if you're brave enough to slam dance in the mosh pit with **her**".

### 87.5 The bugs

1. **The ladder poisoned its own tail.** Every branch was `if (roll < X)` with no
   lower bound. A branch whose pool had no eligible row fell through to a later
   window that also matched, and the execution branch was the widest later window
   (`roll < 0.68`): the first probe found 586 executions against a 5% window. Fixed
   by the availability draw above -- the lesson generalises, and every family with
   an optional branch needs it.
2. **The dispatch list.** `<newspaper>` 76, `<castle>` 20, `<country-adjectival>`
   36 and `<country-possessive>` 24 occurrences leaked; the cases existed but the
   gate did not forward them.
3. **`<hero-royal-name>`** (110 occurrences) had no case in `heroToken` at all.
4. **Column order in the commoner pools.** The feedback snippet was resolved before
   the scenario, so the `<rb>` in "Painted X-rated graffiti of your face with
   <rb>" pointed at nothing (36 leaks). The scenario is resolved first even when the
   card shows the feedback -- the section 57 rule.
5. **A duplicate RNG.** `Rng royalRng_` already existed in include/bl/sim.h with its
   own seed constant from section 47; adding a second one is a compile error
   (`duplicate member royalRng_`, `multiple initializations given for non-static
   member`). Every family added after this one greps the header first.
6. **A dangling `c_str()`.** The seat column was built inside a ternary of two
   temporary `std::string`s; the column name is now hoisted into a local.
7. **A body with no full stop.** The commoner pools end mid-sentence ("Tried to
   touch your crown"), so the card's own tail adds the full stop unless the body
   already ends in one.

### 87.6 Shortcuts

- The rank distribution (half the royals first in line, the rest a rank or two
  down) is the port's own. The real distribution was not read out of the binary.
- The newspaper name is composed, not drawn: the corpus has no newspaper table.
- The hero's execution is triggered by regard alone; the game's own mortality roll
  (`checkDeath`) still runs afterwards.
- School cards fire while the hero's `schooling` flag is set, which the script
  driver enables per life; a royal who never boards a school in the driver never
  sees them.
- A subject is one person per year, reused by every branch that names one, so the
  punished subject and the executed subject of a single year cannot be two people.

### 87.7 Verification

`/tmp/qdir/royres.py` drives thirty seeds across both genders to age sixty in each
of the seventeen countries that have a royal system, with the family and the school
enabled, and reads back every event whose title belongs to the family. The final
run:

```
runs 60 rc failures 0 royal years 2591
  The palace               (none)                                         681
  In the papers            a16_royal-tabloid-scenarios-enc                353
  A royal disgrace         a16_royal-public-disservice-scenarios-enc      332
  A royal duty             a16_royal-public-service-scenarios-enc         319
  An ungrateful subject    a16_royal-commoner-negative-scenarios-enc      241
  An invitation            a16_royal-celebrity-interaction-scenarios-enc  231
  A sentence               a16_royal-punishments-enc                      187
  An execution             a16_royal-executions-enc                        69
  At school                a16_royal-school-positive-scenarios-enc         59
  At school                a16_royal-school-negative-scenarios-enc         55
  A revolt                 a16_royal-executions-enc                        26
  A loyal subject          a16_royal-commoner-positive-scenarios-enc       20
```

Eleven tables are a card's own mark; `a16_royal-house-names-enc` is a setup pool
(the seat and the castle) and is never a card, and the quiet year carries no table


The whole regression is green with the section in place: `allprobes.py` runs

`distinct residue tokens 0 total 0`, `coverage.py` 109 captured / 107 recoverable,
`portgap.py` `ENTRIES 109 rendered-by-port 107 gap 0`, `blsim --script
covpush.json` rc 0 with 33078 bytes of stdout and an empty stderr, and
`bench.sh /tmp/trace_c10.json` reaching age 34 without an abort.

## 88. The anniversary: a family with a vocabulary and no year

Section 57 put relationships on their feet -- hookups, cheating, suspicion, the
nagging road to a wedding -- and left the anniversary one line long:

```cpp
if (h.loverStatus == "married" && fire("a16_anniversary-date-enc", 0.12)) { bump(8); return true; }
```

That line renders one of a hundred date plans and adds eight points. The family
behind it is 565 rows over four tables, and the other three had no path at all:
338 gifts, 116 lines the partner says about a gift, and an eleven row table that
*names* what happened -- the badge the relationship feed carries over the card.
A married year in the port was a restaurant booking with no present, no
reaction, no caption and nothing in the ledger.

This section gives the family a year: one card per married year, drawn from four
ways to spend an anniversary, capped by the family's own badge, and scored in
the relationship meter the section 57 chain already shares.

### 88.1 The family

| table | rows | what it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `a16_anniversary-gift-enc` | 338 | Gift (article included), Cost, Min Age, Max Age, Appreciation Score (-5..5), Hero Gender, Lover Gender, Commonness Score |
| `a16_anniversary-gift-color-enc` | 116 | String, Commonness Score -- what the partner says about the gift, in `<lover>`/`<he/she>` |
| `a16_anniversary-date-enc` | 100 | Activity, Feedback String, Log String, Cost, Min Age, Max Age, Relationship Impact (wired by 57) |
| `a16_anniversary-community-goals-titles-enc` | 11 | Scenario Tag, Option 1..5, Situation Description |

Two tables are pools the hero can take (the date and the gift), one is a pool of
reactions (the colour table), and the last is not a pool of prose at all but the
family's index: every card the family shows in the feed carries one of its eleven
tags, and each tag owns five captions and one sentence of situation.

The two pools that carry prices have opposite shapes. A date is a *price*: costs
run 0, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 65, 80, 90, 100, 120, 150, 180, 200, 300,
400, 500, 700, 1000, and every row pays off with a Relationship Impact of 1..5.
A gift is a *verdict*: the Appreciation Score runs -5..5, so a present can cost
the meter points as well as money, and the pool is mostly jokes -- "a pair of
used socks", "an expired bottle of Tylenol", "a single french fry", "an empty
beer bottle" -- with a few good ones: "a poem", "a home cooked meal", "a coupon
for a handjob". Its gender pair is mostly open -- both/both 291, both/male 20,
both/female 17, male/male 5, male/both 3, male/female 2.

### 88.2 The four ways

The year is a single weighted draw over the four ways an anniversary is spent,
not a ladder of tests. That is deliberate, and it is section 87's lesson applied
before the bug instead of after it: a chain of `if (roll < X)` with no lower
bound lets an unavailable branch fall through into a later window, and the family
would have spent every anniversary doing whatever the tail of the chain happened
to be.

The draw picks a *kind*, and each kind then draws a row from its own pool:

| kind | weight | the card |
|---|---|---|
| date | 10/27 | a row of `a16_anniversary-date-enc` the hero is old enough for and can afford |
| the hero's gift | 7/27 | a row of `a16_anniversary-gift-enc`, the same gates, paid for by the hero |
| the partner's gift | 4/27 | a row of the same table, **no cost gate** -- the partner is paying |
| the night | 6/27 | the port's own text; the family has no pool for it |

A kind whose pool has nothing the hero can take -- too young for every row, too
poor for every price, or a gender gate that excludes them all -- does not fall
through. It becomes the family's own failed-afternoon badge, `OMG_SO_PICKY`, and
the year ends with the day gone. In a hundred runs that is 22 of 278
anniversaries, which is the honest rate at which a married hero has nothing to do.

The gate on every pool is the shared `relEligible`, so the family inherits the
whole column vocabulary section 57 already reads (`Hero Gender`, `Lover Gender`,
`Hero Min Age`/`Hero Max Age`, `Min Age`/`Max Age`, and the rest). The cost
gate is the port's own addition, and it is the one place the family's money
becomes a decision: a hero with nothing in the bank cannot book the anniversary
and gets the picky badge. The `draw` helper takes the cost column as a parameter
precisely so that the partner's gift can opt out of it.

### 88.3 The badge table

Eleven tags, nine of them reachable in a one-card year:

| tag | reached when | what the card shows |
|---|---|---|
| `STRONGER_THAN_EVER` | the date's own Relationship Impact >= 3 | In it for the long haul / Power couple / Unbreakable bond / How lovely / Relationship goals |
| `TOGETHER_FOREVER` | the date's Impact < 3 | Love is in the air / My one and only / Sealed the deal / And they lived happily ever after / Just the two of us |
| `AWW_YOU_SHOULDNT_HAVE` | the hero's gift, Appreciation Score > 0 | Such a sweetheart / Aww, you should't have / Gift giving pro / Straight to the heart / Nailed it |
| `THANKS_BABE` | the partner's gift, Appreciation Score >= 0 | A thoughtful gift / It's the thought that counts / You shouldn't have! / I'll cherish this / So sweet |
| `OH_OKAY_THEN` | the partner's gift, Appreciation Score < 0 | Well that was awkward / That simply won't do / Maybe I shouldn't have / There was no thought / You wanna try again? |
| `HAPPY_ANNIVERSARY_BABE` | the night, a 0.70 success | Mission accomplished / Bow-chicka-wow-wow / A night to remember / Good work all around / I love anniversaries |
| `OKAY_I_GUESS` | the night refused, coin A | I love you too... / Spark is gone / No love in the air / Fine by me / Go to bed |
| `WHAT_ARE_WE_DOING_HERE` | the night refused, coin B | Not in the mood / Went in too cold / Vibes are way off / Am I just some sex bot?! / So unromantic |
| `OMG_SO_PICKY` | every pool for the drawn kind was empty | Indecisive much? / Can't have it all / Decision paralysis / Those are some high standards / The moment has come and went |
| `ONCE_IS_ENOUGH` | -- | "The hero tried to do an activity again too soon": one card a year cannot repeat itself |
| `TURNED_UP_A_NOTCH` | -- | "The hero and their partner were inspired by watching a rewarded video": the port has no rewarded video |

`annBadgeOption(tag, situation, rowOut)` is the whole index: it finds the row
whose `Scenario Tag` matches (case and space insensitive), collects whichever of
`Option 1`..`Option 5` are non-empty, states the row's `Situation Description`,
and draws one caption. The card's title is that caption, the feed line carries
the situation, and the ledger gets both:

```
Badge: Nailed it - The hero gave their partner a thoughtful gift.
Our relationship stands at 63% after 4 anniversaries and 3 gifts.
```

A card whose gift the partner did not want has no tag to carry -- the table has
no fifth "bad present" row -- so it takes the gift's own name as its title, with
"was not impressed" in the log. `a chewed up pencil ` in the corpus ends in a
space, hence the `trim` on every gift name.

### 88.4 The tokens

The family speaks through one pronoun pair and one back-reference, and both
needed the care section 57 already learned:

* **`<lover>`, `<he/she>`, `<his/her>` are the partner** -- the *other*
  person, not the hero. Every pool is written from the hero's side, so
  `pronounOtherSet_` is set and `pronounOtherFemale_` is pinned to
  `h.loverFemale` for the whole card. Get that backwards and every husband
  becomes "she" in a line the hero is supposedly reading about himself.
* **The date's `Feedback String` must resolve before its `Log String`.** The
  log is the first-person plural twin of the feed and points back into it with
  `<rb>`/`<rb2>` -- "went to the happiest place `<on Earth/in the world>`" then
  "We went to the happiest place `<rb>`". Resolve the log first and the
  back-reference has nothing to point at.
* **`<num5-27>` and friends need no work.** `numberToken` (section 22) already
  covers `<number:natural10-12000>`, `<number:currency120-5000>`, the legacy
  `<num2-5>`/`<currency...>` forms and the `_roundup` suffixes, so the
  handful of log strings that carry one resolve like any other token.
* **The partner's line about a gift** is drawn from the colour table by
  `Commonness Score` and appended after the hero's own sentence, which is why a
  card can read "I accepted it." and then be told about the zombie apocalypse by
  the spouse.

### 88.5 What it caught

This is the first section in a while whose bug list is short, and the reason is
worth stating: the family has exactly one cross-table hand-off (the date's own
`<rb>`) and no shared counters, so there was no token plumbing to get wrong.
The bugs it did have:

1. **Cards with no source table.** The night and the failed afternoon have no
   pool row, so `out.table` stayed empty and the two most common cards of the
   family appeared to come from nowhere. The badge row *is* their source, and
   `annBadgeOption` now reports its index so the card can name
   `a16_anniversary-community-goals-titles-enc` as the table it came from. The
   first probe run reported 84 cards as `(none)`; the second reports none.
2. **The probe's own taxonomy.** The first two histograms called
   `OKAY_I_GUESS`'s captions part of the angry night, which made a correct card
   look like a badge/text mismatch: "No love in the air" and "Spark is gone"
   belong to the reluctant *refusal* row, not the angry one. The fix was to the
   probe, and the check it left behind -- every card's badge family must agree
   with the text in its log -- is now an assertion: 0 mismatches over 278 cards.
3. **A gift name with a trailing space** (`a chewed up pencil `), which would have
   produced a double space in the middle of a sentence. Trimmed.
4. **No `lowerFirst` anywhere in the port.** Every card here joins two strings
   with the pool's own sentence ("you and Adele " + "Grabbed nets and ran..."),
   so the family carries a four-line lambda that lowercases the first byte.
5. **A negative score column through `num()`.** `Appreciation Score` is the
   first column the port reads that is negative *and* decides a branch, so
   `OH_OKAY_THEN` is the assertion that `num` parses a leading minus: six cards
   in the run, and that branch is the only way to reach them.

### 88.6 Shortcuts

* **45% of a married year is the anniversary.** The family carries no rate
  column; a year is a card, and the rest of the married years belong to the
  section 57 chain -- hookups, cheating, nags, counseling, breakup.
* **The four weights are the port's own** (10/7/4/6 out of 27). The corpus has no
  table that says how often a couple goes out, gives a present, or spends the
  night together.
* **The night has no pool at all.** The two refusal texts are the port's own,
  because the corpus's refusal pool (`a16_make-love-rejections-enc`, 193 rows) is
  the *partner's* excuses -- "`<he/she>` says `<he/she>` is too
  `<exhausted/tired/sleepy>`" -- and the two badges the family offers are about
  the hero turning the partner down instead.
* **A repeat cannot happen inside one year**, so `ONCE_IS_ENOUGH` has no path,
  and `TURNED_UP_A_NOTCH` needs a rewarded video the port does not model.
* **The night's success is a flat 0.70** with +6 relationship and +4 happiness;
  the refusal is -6 and -3, and the two refusal badges are split by a coin.
* **One card per year, one subject.** The ledger counters (`anniversaries`,
  `annGifts`) are the only state the family adds to the hero.

### 88.7 Verification

`annres.py` runs 100 lives to age 80 with relationships enabled
(`relationship: true` in the script spec, which turns `makeRelationships` on)
across the seventeen countries of `a16_country-royal-systems-enc`, and reads
back every event whose log carries the family's ledger line -- the one line no
other family writes. The final run:

```
runs 100 rc failures 0 anniversary years 278 lives with one 40
phase by tag: TOGETHER_FOREVER 75, HAPPY_ANNIVERSARY_BABE 45, AWW_YOU_SHOULDNT_HAVE 44,
  THANKS_BABE 31, OMG_SO_PICKY 22, gift-name 20, STRONGER_THAN_EVER 18,
  WHAT_ARE_WE_DOING_HERE 9, OKAY_I_GUESS 8, OH_OKAY_THEN 6
card sources: a16_anniversary-gift-enc 101, a16_anniversary-date-enc 93,
  a16_anniversary-community-goals-titles-enc 84
distinct badge captions 42 of 45
badge/text mismatches 0
RESIDUE 0 []
```

Forty of the hundred lives reached a marriage and an anniversary at all, which is
the corpus's own rate: the section 57 chain ends a relationship that falls under
30, and most heroes who do marry marry late. Forty-two of the forty-five captions
of the nine reachable tags appeared; the three that did not are the rarest draws
-- a caption is one of five, drawn uniformly, and 278 cards is not enough to
cover every corner of that table. All four tables are a card's own mark, and no
card is left without one.

Nine cards, one per branch:

```
date           And they lived happily ever after
               For your anniversary, you and Maylor grabbed nets and ran through the
               fields capturing and releasing wild butterflies.
               We grabbed nets and ran through the fields capturing and releasing
               wild butterflies.
gift (hero)    Nailed it
               For your anniversary, you gave Mary a home cooked meal.
               I gave Mary a home cooked meal and Mary loved it.
gift (hero)    A pair of used underwear with skid marks
               For your anniversary, you gave Mary a pair of used underwear with
               skid marks.
               I gave Mary a pair of used underwear with skid marks and Mary was
               not impressed.
gift (partner) It's the thought that counts
               For your anniversary, Adele gave you all of Lord of the Rings.
               I accepted it. Adele says that if the zombie apocalypse ever came to
               pass, she would make sure you're never infected with anything but her love.
night          Mission accomplished
               For your anniversary, you and Adele spent a night to remember.
               We had a night to remember.
refusal A      Fine by me
               You turned Whit-Leigh down on your anniversary.
               I was not in the mood and Whit-Leigh said 'I love you too...' and
               went to bed.
refusal B      Vibes are way off
               You turned Mary down on your anniversary.
               I was not in the mood and Mary said the vibes were way off.

               You could not decide what to do for your anniversary and the day
               went by.
               I ran out of ideas and we did nothing at all.
```

The whole regression is green with the section in place: `allprobes.py` runs
thirty-three probes at residue 0 (section 90 adds `convres.py` to the list),
`rescensus.py` `distinct residue tokens 0 total 0`, `coverage.py` 109 captured /
107 recoverable, `portgap.py` `ENTRIES 109 rendered-by-port 107 gap 0`, `blsim
--script covpush.json` rc 0 with an empty stderr, and `bench.sh
/tmp/trace_c10.json` reaching age 34 without an abort.

## 89. The gift: one shelf, four price tables, and a partner who can only refuse

Section 88 gave the couple a year. This section gives it a shop. The gift family
is three files and 478 rows, and it is the first family in this port whose card
text is not in the corpus at all: the shop writes its own prose, and the tables
contribute a name, a price, two appreciation scores and - at the expensive end -
the sentence a partner uses to hand the thing back.

### 89.1 The family

`a16_gifts-enc` is the shelf. 383 rows, twelve columns:

| column | what it holds |
|--------|---------------|
| `Gift` | the name as the shop writes it: `Rolex watch`, `diamond earrings`, `SlimFast shake mix` |
| `Is Singular` | `x` on 337 rows; the 46 blanks take no article |
| `Use Them` | `x` on 33 (the wearables: the jacket you put on, the sunglasses you put on) |
| `Is Flowers` | `x` on 12 - every bouquet in the table |
| `Cost` | 0 to 50000, 46 distinct values, dense below 35 and then a long tail (1500, 1600, 2000, 4500, 10000, 50000) |
| `Male Appreciation Score` | -5 to 5, no zero anywhere in the column |
| `Female Appreciation Score` | the same range, and 184 of the 383 rows disagree with the male one |
| `Min Age` / `Max Age` | 1 to 65 / 2 to 80, with a blank Max Age reading as open |
| `Commonness Score` | 1 to 5 - the shelf's own weight |
| `Can Be Shoplifted` | `x` on 267 |
| `Sack Exclusive` | `x` on 85, and those 85 rows are exactly the cost-0 rows |

The last two columns are the section. `Can Be Shoplifted` is the flag that
decides whether an unaffordable gift is reachable at all, and `Sack Exclusive`
is Santa's sack - every free row in the table belongs to a Christmas the port
does not model, so the shop skips them and a broke hero is left with the lifting
branch or nothing. 210 of the 383 rows cost 20 or less, 85 of which are the
sack, so the affordable shelf is 125 rows.

Two of those rows are worth quoting whole:

`@
Gift                 Is Singular Use Them Is Flowers Cost Male Female MinAge MaxAge Commonness Can Be Shoplifted Sack Exclusive
Rolex watch          x                       x                 10000  5    5       16            5          x
shrunken head        x                                         50000  2    -5      18            3          x
`@

The two refusal pools are the only prose the family ships:
`a16_gift-rejections-house-enc` (48 rows) and
`a16_gift-rejections-vehicle-enc` (47 rows). Both are `Excuse, Prideful,
Crazy, ... Min Value, Max Value, Child Recipient Only, Parent Recipient Only,
Lover Recipient Only, Min Relationship, Max Relationship, Recipient Min Age,
Recipient Max Age`. The house pool splits 22 `Prideful` / 26 `Crazy` and
the vehicle pool 24 / 23, and no row in either table carries both flags or
neither: the trait is a partition, not a score.

| pool | value window | relationship | recipient age |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------|
| house | Min Value 150000, Max Value 750000 | Min Relationship 70, Max Relationship 50 and 30 | Min Age 18 and 40, Max Age 20 and 23 |
| vehicle (Car) | 7000 to 100000 | as above | as above |
| vehicle (Boat) | 30000 to 1000000 | as above | as above |
| vehicle (Plane) | 100000 to 1000000 | as above | as above |

The vehicle table carries a flag per kind - `Car` on 35 rows, `Boat` on 34,
`Plane` on 33 - so one row is written for one kind of vehicle, and its
`<Kind> Min Value` / `<Kind> Max Value` columns are the window that row
answers to. The sentences are what the section is for, and they all end in a
refusal:

`@
<He/She> said <he/she> wants to buy <his/her> own home.
<He/She> said <he/she> doesn't need your <hand-me-downs/charity>.
<He/She> said <he/she> couldn't accept a house that <nice/fancy/pricey/costly>.
<He/She> said <he/she> doesn't feel like the quality of your relationship is good enough to justify a gift of this magnitude.
<He/She> said the only thing <he/she> wants to fly is a kite.
<He/She> said <he/she> wouldn't know where to dock it.
`@

There is no acceptance pool and no shoplifting consequence table anywhere in the
corpus: a grep for `shoplift`, `loved it` and `gift you gave` over the
whole of `gamedata_plain` finds nothing else in this family. Both of those
voices are the port's own, and section 89.6 says where they stop.

The four price tables the pools are answered from are the ones the earlier
sections already read, and each of them breaks a rule the other three keep:

| table | rows | price column | note |
|-------|------|--------------|------|
| `a16_house-types-enc` | 29 | none - `Price Score` | section 66's landlord family already charges `Price Score * 60000` plus jitter |
| `a16_car-models-enc` | 186 | `Cost` as `$44,990` | the only price table with no `Commonness Score` column at all |
| `a16_watercraft-enc` | wired by 81 | `Cost` | already in `kTables` since the boat section |
| `a16_aircraft-enc` | 59 | `Cost` as `$304,000` | `Descriptive Name Override`, and 20 `Luxury Only` rows |

### 89.2 The two paths

`giftYear` hangs off the couple's year, right after the anniversary line in
`relationshipYear` (src/sim.cpp:23210), so a married anniversary card still
wins the year it fires. The whole card is one of two paths, and the shop is the
fallback:

| path | gate | what decides the outcome |
|------|------|--------------------------|
| the grand gesture | `h.money >= 100000` and a 0.35 coin | the refusal pool: a matching row means the partner refuses, an empty pool means the gift is taken |
| the shop | everything else, then a 0.30 coin for the year | the row's own `Cost` against the wallet, then `Can Be Shoplifted`, then the appreciation score |

The gesture walks the four kinds in a random order - house, car, boat, plane -
and tries each until one yields a card, because a table can be unaffordable at
one end (an aircraft is never under 43500, a house never under 150000) and a
partner can be outside every window. The price comes from the kind's own source:
`Price Score * 60000` for a house with the same `below(20000)` jitter the
landlord family uses, and the `Cost` column for the other three. The item name
is `Descriptive Name Override` when the table has one and it is non-empty
(`Cessna 172S`), otherwise `Make` plus `Model` (`Kia Telluride`,
`Lexus IS-500`), otherwise `Type` (`sailing cutter`, `geodesic`).

The shop is three filters and a weighted pick. `Sack Exclusive` rows are out
(the Christmas sack is not a shop), the partner's age has to fall inside
`Min Age` / `Max Age`, and then the shelf splits in two: everything at or
under the wallet is affordable, everything above it that carries
`Can Be Shoplifted` is reachable. The affordable half is picked with
`weightedPickOf` on `Commonness Score` - the shelf's own weight, so the
common trinkets dominate and the Rolex stays rare - and only when that half is
empty does the lifting branch open, on a 0.45 coin.

The outcome is then the row's own two numbers and two flags:

| branch | corpus input | what the card says |
|--------|--------------|--------------------|
| bought | `Cost` | `money -= cost`, `I gave <lover> <what>` (or `I sent` when `Is Flowers`) |
| lifted, clean | `Can Be Shoplifted` | `karma -4`, `I lifted <what> for <lover> without paying` |
| lifted, caught | the port's own 0.25 | `karma -12`, relationship -4, happiness -3, `I was caught lifting <what> for <lover>` |
| the reaction | `Male` / `Female Appreciation Score`, read by the partner's gender | `>= 4` loved it (+3 happiness, +score), `> 0` liked it (+1), else hated it (-3) |

and the article comes from `Is Singular`: `a Lush bath set`, `an oil
diffuser`, `an Xbox Series X`, but `Beats headphones`, `Canon binoculars`
and `SlimFast shake mix` with nothing in front of them.

### 89.3 The refusals

The corpus answers the expensive half with a sentence, and the sentence is
chosen by a trait the corpus itself declares: every row of both pools is flagged
`Prideful` or `Crazy` and never both. The port has no such traits, so it
maps them onto the two scores the couple already keeps: `loverCraziness` was
already drawn by `relationshipYear` for the hookup card, and section 89 draws
`loverPride` next to it, both 0 to 100. A partner at or above 50 is proud, at
or above 50 on the other is crazy, and the pool is then filtered by that flag,
by the kind's own flag, by the value window, by `Min` / `Max Relationship`
against the current score and by the recipient's age.

The consequence of that mapping is the section's interesting result: a partner
who is neither proud nor crazy has no row to refuse with, and the port takes the
gift. Over the probe's 100 lives the two pools were read 50 times and the
acceptance branch fired 6 - which is roughly the 1-in-4 the two independent
coin flips predict, and it is also the shape of any table that partitions a
population instead of scoring it.

Two of the recipient flags the port cannot honour: `Child Recipient Only` and
`Parent Recipient Only` need a child or a parent to hand a house to, and this
port's families are the hero's siblings and children only. They are skipped,
which leaves the `Lover Recipient Only` rows and the unmarked ones.

### 89.4 The tokens

This family needs no new token. The refusal sentences are resolved by machinery
the earlier sections already installed:

- `<He/She>` and `<His/Her>` are the capital twin of the pronoun pair
  (src/sim.cpp:1764), so the sentence starts with the partner's gender and
  continues in lower case.
- `<hand-me-downs/charity>` and `<nice/fancy/pricey/costly>` are inline
  slash lists, resolved by the same pass that draws `<a/b>` everywhere else.
- the card's own prose goes through `money()`, so a house in Japan prints in
  yen and the probe's `90,000` above is the same number in another country.
- `<rb>` is not used: no pool sentence points back at another line.

`heroToken` gained nothing either - the gift is about the partner, and the
port already forwards `lover` (src/sim.cpp:22980) for exactly this.

### 89.5 What it caught

Seven things, five of them real bugs and two of them rules the corpus keeps that
the earlier price readers had never been forced to notice:

1. `a Xbox Series X`. The article rule in the shop tested for a vowel and
   wrote `a` in front of a name that is pronounced `eks`. The fix is the
   heuristic the port now carries: vowels and `x` take `an`, and the
   shortcut line says what that gives up (`a ukulele` is written `an
   ukulele` and the shop does not carry one).
2. the karma route. The first version wrote `h.karma -= 4` directly, and the
   demo driver's `deltas` object - which reports the `AgeUp` fields, not the
   hero - showed 0 for every lifting card. src/script.cpp:762 applies
   `ev.karma` and then clamps all five stats, so a direct mutation is applied
   but invisible. The card now sets `out.karma` and the probe asserts -4 on a
   clean lift and -12 on a caught one.
3. `a airboat`. The property prose had a hard-coded article while the shop
   path had the real one. Both now share `article()`.
4. the house has no `Cost` column. The price tables read like one shape until
   this family needed a house: `a16_house-types-enc` prices itself with
   `Price Score`, and the only code that knows what one point is worth is
   section 66's landlord purchase (src/sim.cpp:10176). The gift reuses that
   formula rather than inventing a second one.
5. `a16_car-models-enc` has no `Commonness Score`. Every other price table
   in this port has one, so `weightedPickOf` cannot be called on it and the
   car is picked uniformly. The table in 89.1 is the census of that.
6. the `Is Singular` blank is "takes no article", not "plural". The 46 blank
   rows include mass nouns (`SlimFast shake mix`, `CBD oil`) and brand names
   (`Altoids`) as well as the real plurals (`Beats headphones`,
   `diamond earrings`), so the flag is read as an article switch and never as
   a plurality test.
7. the trait partition. Before the trait map the pool was filtered by value and
   relationship alone, and the pool then answered for partners who should have
   had no sentence at all. The flags are not a score, and reading them as one is
   what 89.3 is about.

### 89.6 Shortcuts

1. the rate and the year. `giftYear` fires on 0.30 of the couple's remaining
   years, after the anniversary card has had its 0.45. Neither number is in the
   corpus; the family has no year column at all.
2. the grand gesture's gate: `money >= 100000` and a 0.35 coin. The corpus's
   only clue is the value windows, whose floors are 7000 (a car) and 150000 (a
   house).
3. the shoplifting consequence: `Can Be Shoplifted` is a permission, not a
   consequence. The karma -4, the 0.25 caught branch, the -12 and the guard's
   sentence are the port's own, because no table in `gamedata_plain` carries a
   shoplifting outcome.
4. the appreciation reaction ("loved it", "liked it", "hated it") is the port's
   own phrasing of the two score columns. No table carries the partner's reply.
5. the trait map is a threshold. `loverPride >= 50` and `loverCraziness >=
   50` stand in for two flags the corpus has and the port does not, and a
   partner's two scores are one draw each for the life, not a per-card roll.
6. the acceptance branch is flat prose. A partner with neither trait has no pool
   row, and the corpus has no text for a partner who says yes to a house, so the
   card reads `I bought <lover> <what> as a gift` with a fixed +12 / +5.
7. one card a year, and the property attempt is never both. A year that refuses
   a house does not also visit the shop.

### 89.7 Verification

`/tmp/qdir/giftres.py` drives 100 lives - seeds 1 to 50 in both genders, to
age 80, over the 17 countries of `a16_country-royal-systems-enc`, with
relationships on and a wealth switch (business, politics, office, actor) cycled
per seed so the expensive half is reached at all. It selects a card by its own
ledger line (`I have given N gift(s) and lifted N`), classifies it by the
body, asserts the karma and happiness the branch owes, checks the ledger is
monotonic inside a life, and scans every string for an unresolved token:

## 90. The conversations: one audience column, a listener the port had to invent, and a six-sided coin for tolerance

Sections 88 and 89 belonged to the couple. This one belongs to the family around
it. `a16_conversations-enc` is a single file of 345 rows and it is the first
family in this port whose card has three moving parts at once: who is listening,
what the hero says, and whether the listener can take it.

### 90.1 The family

`a16_conversations-enc` is nine columns and 345 rows:

| column | what it holds |
|--------|---------------|
| `Audience` | blank on 247 rows; `Lover` 28, `Child` 26, `Daughter` 13, `Son` 12, `Parent` 10, `Parents` 7, plus two rows whose value carries a trailing space |
| `Conversation` | the topic. Non-blank on all 345 rows and 342 distinct; `the birds and the bees` appears three times and `how tampons work` twice |
| `Hero Min Age` / `Hero Max Age` | the hero's own window. Min blank on 53 rows and otherwise 3 to 65, clustered at 12 (46 rows), 18 (45), 15 (40), 10 (34) and 14 (24). Max blank on 315 |
| `Audience Min Age` / `Audience Max Age` | the listener's window. Min blank on 20 rows and clustered at 12 (61), 15 (46), 18 (45), 10 (37) and 5 (25). Max blank on 295 |
| `Controversy Score` | 1 to 5: 101 / 95 / 83 / 51 / 14 rows, and one blank row |
| `Clean` | `x` on 289 rows, blank on 56 |
| `Holiday` | `x` on 27 rows |

Four rows, quoted, because between them they are the whole table:

```
Child      | the importance of using a condom      | | | 15 | 21 | 1 |   |
Child      | why it is important to do chores      | | |  6 | 18 | 4 | x |
           | how Pink Floyd is better than Led Zeppelin | 12 | | 12 | | 3 | x |
Parents    | the handcuffs <I/you> found in <mommy's/daddy's> drawer,
           | and why <I/you> never get to play with them | 2 | 9 | | | 2 | |
```

The two windows are the design. `Hero Min Age` says when the hero is old
enough to raise the subject at all (the birds and the bees at 12, the will at
65), `Audience Min Age` says when the person hearing it is old enough for it,
and `Clean` separates the 56 rows that should never reach a child. The score
is what the listener does with the subject once it is out.

### 90.2 The listener

The corpus's `Audience` column names six relatives. The port has three of
them. `life.family` holds the parents and the siblings (a sibling is
`big`/`little brother`/`sister` with a first name, and its age is 2 to 6
when the hero is older or 2 to 3 at birth), and `loverName` holds the partner.
There is no child list anywhere in the port, because the hero of this
construction never has children of their own - so the 51 `Child` /
`Daughter` / `Son` rows have no literal listener and are read as the
younger sibling instead:

| `Audience` | who the port picks | the ear's kind |
|--------------|--------------------|----------------|
| blank (247 rows) | anybody in the room | `a` |
| `Lover` | the partner, when `relationshipOn` and the name is set | `l` |
| `Parent` | `my mother` or `my father` (the port keeps no parent names, so the relation is the name) | `p` |
| `Parents` | both at once, one ear called `my parents` | `P` |
| `Child` / `Son` / `Daughter` | the younger sibling, gender-matched for Son and Daughter | `c` |

Every listener is one `struct Ear` with a name, an age, a gender and a kind.
Three gates then filter the 345 rows: `heroOk` reads `Hero Min Age` /
`Hero Max Age` against the hero, `earOk` reads `Audience Min Age` /
`Audience Max Age` against that ear (a blank or zero column is open), and
`kindOk` matches the audience word - blank fits anybody, `Lover` needs the
`l` ear, `Parent` and `Parents` the `p` and `P` ears, and
`Son` / `Daughter` also check the sibling's gender. The surviving pairs
(row, ear) are picked uniformly.

The `Clean` column is read in exactly one place, as `not in front of the
children`: `if (!t.flag(r, "Clean") && ears[e].kind == 'c') continue;`. The
partner and the parents get the whole table; a sibling is never told about
anal bleaching or the drawer with the handcuffs in it.

### 90.3 The coin

The topic is resolved with the listener's pronouns (the card is written from the
hero's side, so `<we/you>` has to become `we` for a parent and stay the
hero's word for a sibling), and then one roll decides how it landed:

```
const int score = std::max(1, int(t.num(row, "Controversy Score")));
const bool awkward = int(relRng_.below(6)) < score;
```

A six-sided die and the score as the number of faces that go badly. A score-1
topic (the best movie we saw this year) passes five times in six; a score-5
topic (a sexting conversation found on someone's phone) passes once in six.

Measured over 1,517 cards in 200 lives:

| `Controversy Score` | cards | awkward | measured | expected | delta |
|--------|-------|---------|----------|----------|-------|
| 1 | 527 | 99 | 0.188 | 0.167 | +0.021 |
| 2 | 419 | 124 | 0.296 | 0.333 | -0.037 |
| 3 | 356 | 186 | 0.522 | 0.500 | +0.022 |
| 4 | 198 | 135 | 0.682 | 0.667 | +0.015 |
| 5 | 17 | 14 | 0.824 | 0.833 | -0.010 |

The card itself: title is the topic with its first letter raised, body is
`I told my mother about the best movie we saw so far this year.` - plus
`, and it did not go well.` on the bad roll - and the narrative flips with
it, `My father listened to my thoughts on ...` or `I brought ... up with my
mother and regretted it.` Happiness swings a point, the partner loses two
relationship points and gains one on a good night, and the ledger line is
`I have had N conversations, M of them awkward.`

### 90.4 The tokens

The topic column uses sixteen distinct brackets. Six are inline slash lists the
port already handles (`<pea/Lego/marble/...>`, `<McDonald's/Burger King/Taco
Bell>`, `<willy/ding dong/wiener/pee-pee/wee-wee>`, `<nose/ear>`,
`<mommy's/daddy's>`, the eight-way reality-show list), `<musician>` already
resolves through `referenceToken` (src/sim.cpp:1659), and eight are
perspective pairs. Five of those eight were missing from `kPairs`, because
the corpus writes both sides of the same pronoun and the port only ever tells a
card in the first person:

| token | rows | was | now |
|-------|------|-----|-----|
| `<we/you>` | 38 | not a pair | `we` |
| `<our/your>` | 38 | not a pair | `our` |
| `<I/you>` | 13 | not a pair | `I` |
| `<my/your>` | 7 | not a pair | `my` |
| `<me/you>` | 1 | not a pair | `me` |
| `<he/she>` | 3 | resolved against the listener | unchanged |
| `<his/her>` | 6 | resolved against the listener | unchanged |
| `<musician2>` | 2 | no handler at all | the row is skipped |

The last row is the one that stayed a shortcut: `<musician2>` has no resolver
in the port (a search for the literal name finds nothing), so instead of
printing a raw bracket the card checks `topic.find('<') != std::string::npos`
after resolving and walks away. Two rows of 345 are unreachable that way, and
the probe asserts no bracket ever reaches the output.

### 90.5 What it caught

The port's own gaps, in the order they showed up:

- the five missing perspective pairs, and that four of the six inline lists on
  the topic column are the ones the family already needed elsewhere -
  `a16_sibling-arguments-enc` and `a16_murders-enc` both use `<I/you>`,
  so the 13 rooms this adds are shared with two families still unwired;
- `<musician2>` has no handler, so the two rows using it are skipped rather
  than printed with a bracket;
- the probe's first title check compared the resolved title against the raw row
  text and reported drift on every token row; the honest check compares the
  head before the first bracket and the tail after the last one;
- a listener classifier of `'lover' if who in joined or True` is meaningless;
  the second pass (no partner at all) is the only honest way to isolate the
  sibling ear, and it shows 318 sibling conversations, none of them on a
  non-`Clean` row;
- `Clean` is not a curiosity column - it is the child gate, and it is the
  only column in the family whose meaning is a rule rather than a value;
- the `Audience` column carries two trailing-space variants, so the audience
  match trims.

### 90.6 Shortcuts

- `conversationYear` fires at 0.22 of a year, the port's own rate; the corpus
  has no frequency column anywhere in the family;
- the listener for `Child` / `Son` / `Daughter` is the younger sibling,
  because the port's hero has no children. All 51 of those rows are reachable,
  which the probe confirms (15 of them land in the no-partner pass);
- tolerance is the rest of a six-sided die; nothing in the corpus says the
  score is a probability, only that it is 1 to 5;
- one person hears one topic a year, and the topic is drawn uniformly rather
  than by any weight - the family has no `Commonness Score` column;
- the two `<musician2>` rows are never spoken;
- a `Holiday` row is treated like any other topic. The flag is carried in the
  table but the port has no holiday calendar to gate it against, so it is not
  read at all.

### 90.7 Verification

`/tmp/qdir/convres.py` runs 200 lives - seeds 1 to 50 in both genders, to age
80, across the 17 countries of `a16_country-royal-systems-enc` - in two passes,
one with a partner and one without. It selects every event whose table is
`a16_conversations-enc` and checks the row index, the listener named in the
body, the title against the row's own topic (bracket-free at the head and the
tail), the awkward sentence against the narrative, `deltas.karma == 0`, the
ledger line's monotonicity inside a life, and that no bracket reaches any
string:

```

score 1: 527 cards awkward 99  0.188 expected 0.167
score 2: 419 cards awkward 124 0.296 expected 0.333
score 3: 356 cards awkward 186 0.522 expected 0.500
score 4: 198 cards awkward 135 0.682 expected 0.667
score 5:  17 cards awkward  14 0.824 expected 0.833
sibling listeners (no-partner pass) 318 of which on a non-Clean row 0
rows used 250 of 345
mismatches 0
RESIDUE 0 []
```

Two cards, one bad roll and one good one:

```
row 249 | the best movie <we/you> saw so far this year
  The best movie we saw so far this year
  I told my mother about the best movie we saw so far this year, and it did not go well.
  I brought the best movie we saw so far this year up with my mother and regretted it.

row 285 | the average intelligence of people who enjoy watching <The Bachelor/...>
  The average intelligence of people who enjoy watching The Bachelorette
  I told my mother about the average intelligence of people who enjoy watching The Bachelorette.
  My mother listened to my thoughts on the average intelligence of people who enjoy watching The Bachelorette.
```

And two that are only reachable through the port's own substitute listener:

```
row 15 audience=Child | why you don't ask a woman with a big belly if she is pregnant
  I told Pink about why you don't ask a woman with a big belly if she is pregnant, and it did not go well.

row 342 clean=False | whether or not it is okay to dye <our/your> gray pubes
  I told Ladye about whether or not it is okay to dye our gray pubes, and it did not go well.
```

The whole regression is green with the section in place: `allprobes.py` runs
thirty-four probes at residue 0 (section 91 adds `socres.py` to the list),
`rescensus.py` `distinct residue tokens 0 total 0`, `coverage.py` 109
captured / 107 recoverable, `portgap.py` `ENTRIES 109 rendered-by-port 107
gap 0`, `blsim --script covpush.json` rc 0 with an empty stderr, and
`bench.sh /tmp/trace_c10.json` reaching age 34 without an abort.


## 91. The social media year: one account, six tables, and a handle nobody could name

Section 90 gave the hero a listener. This one gives him an audience. Seven tables of
`a16_social` had never been read by the port - the only member of the family it had
ever touched was the seven-row channel list, wired long ago as a source of social media
names - and together they are a complete year of its own: a channel the hero picks in
his teens, an account that grows, five ways a year can go, and a second family
(`a16_username`, 413 rows over three files) that exists only to give a stranger a
name.

### 91.1 The family

| table | rows | columns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a16_social-media-channels-enc` | 7 | Channel, Likes Coefficient, Followers Coefficient, Promotion Followers Coefficient, Promotion Monetization Coefficient, Post Type, Post Verb, Post Description Present, Post Description Past, Followers Term, Friends Min Age, Friends Max Age |
| `a16_social-media-post-types-enc` | 53 | Post Type, Scenario, Log Version, Add Video, Appeal Score, Impacted by Looks, Impacted by Smarts, Viral Score, then one column per channel |
| `a16_social-media-troll-inbounds-enc` | 28 | Scenario, Log Version, Is Reply, Twitch Exempt, Twitch Only |
| `a16_social-media-hacks-enc` | 26 | Scenario, Log Version, Damage Score, Both Parents Alive, Has Lover, then one column per channel |
| `a16_social-media-promotion-products-enc` | 148 | Product, Description, Compensation Score, Min Age, Appeal Score, Twitch Exempt |
| `a16_social-media-channels-of-collabstrings-enc` | 47 | String, Engagement Score, Virality, Controversy Score, Commonness Score |
| `a16_username-structure-enc` | 18 | Structure |
| `a16_username-adjectives-enc` | 195 | Adjective, Gender, Min Age, Max Age |
| `a16_username-nouns-enc` | 200 | Noun, Gender, Min Age, Max Age |

The channel table is the spine. A channel is not a name here, it is a **window**: the
`Friends Min Age` and `Friends Max Age` columns bound who uses it, and the port read
them the way the corpus wrote them - Facebook 50 and up, Instagram 18-40, TikTok 13-18,
Twitter 25-45, YouTube 13-30, Twitch 13-70, OnlyFans 18 and up. A fourteen-year-old can
only land on TikTok, YouTube or Twitch; a fifty-five-year-old cannot land on TikTok at
all. The same table carries the arithmetic (`Likes Coefficient`,
`Followers Coefficient`, `Followers Term` - followers everywhere except YouTube and
OnlyFans, which call them subscribers) and the noun a post is described with
(`Post Type`: post, video, tweet or livestream).

Each of the three event tables then carries one column per channel, an `x` meaning
this can happen here: post-types has Facebook 21, Instagram 20, Twitter 19, Twitch 13,
YouTube 12, OnlyFans 10, TikTok 9; hacks has Facebook 26, Twitter 25, Instagram 24,
TikTok 14, YouTube 13, Twitch 4. A hack card is therefore several times more likely to
be about a Facebook account than a Twitch one, and the port did not have to invent
that - it reads the columns.

Two tables are gates rather than vocabulary. `a16_social-media-hacks-enc` has
`Both Parents Alive` and `Has Lover`, so a hacking card can require that the hero
still has something to lose. `a16_social-media-troll-inbounds-enc` has `Twitch Only`
(10 rows) and `Twitch Exempt` (15), and `a16_social-media-promotion-products-enc`
has `Twitch Exempt` on 18 of its 148 rows plus a `Min Age` (16, 18 or 21 on the 34
rows that carry one), so a beer brand will not offer a sponsorship to a fifteen-year-
old.

What the family does not have is prose for the two oldest branches. A post, a troll and
a hack all ship a `Scenario` and a `Log Version`. A sponsorship ships a product, a
description and two scores; a collaboration ships an activity string and two scores.
Those two cards are the port's own sentences, and 91.6 says so.

### 91.2 The account

The channel is drawn once, in the first year the hero is old enough, from the rows
whose `Friends Min Age` / `Friends Max Age` window contains his age - so the draw is
already biased by the corpus's own idea of who uses what - and stored in
`h.socialChannel`. Every later card in that life comes from the same channel: a hero
who drew Facebook at fifteen is still on Facebook at forty.

The hero's own handle is generated once, at the same moment, by `makeUsername`, and
kept in `h.socialUsername`. It is eighteen formats from
`a16_username-structure-enc` - `<first-name><surname>`,
`<first-name>_<surname>`, `<surname><first-name>`, `<first-name><num1-999>`,
`<adjective><first-name>`, `<adjective><num1950-2005>` and twelve more - filled
from the two word pools, each word gated by its own `Gender`, `Min Age` and
`Max Age` (the adjective horny is 18 and up, the noun aunt is female only). A word
that does not fit the hero is not drawn, and a token that cannot be filled is dropped
rather than printed: the port would rather lose a letter of a handle than show a
bracket.

### 91.3 The five ways

The year is one weighted draw over the branches that have something to say, exactly as
section 87 taught - never a bare `roll < X` ladder, because a branch whose pool is
empty would fall through into a later window and hand the year to the wrong table.

| kind | weight | pool | empty when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| post | 12 | post-types, rows flagged for this channel | never |
| trolled | 8 | troll-inbounds, minus the `Twitch Only` rows on other channels | rarely |
| promotion | 6 | promotion-products, skipping `Twitch Exempt` on Twitch and a `Min Age` above the hero | young hero on Twitch |
| collaboration | 5 | collaboration strings | never |
| hacked | 4 | hacks, rows flagged for this channel and passing both gates | hero with no partner and no parents |

A post is worth a number: `likes = (Appeal + Viral) * Likes Coefficient * 100` and
`followers += likes * Followers Coefficient * (1 + Viral * 0.5) * 10`. The corpus
ships the two coefficients and no formula at all, so the shape of that line, and the
100 and the 10, are the port's; what is not the port's is that the viral score
multiplies the gain, and that OnlyFans pays no more per view than Facebook does. A
viral score of 4 or more also writes a sentence into the log - The post went viral. -
and hands the hero one more point of happiness.

| branch | what it moves |
| --- | --- |
| post | `money` no, `happiness` by the `Appeal Score` (plus one when viral), the account by the likes line |
| trolled | `happiness` -3 |
| promotion | `money += Compensation Score * 2500 * Promotion Monetization Coefficient`, `happiness` by the `Appeal Score` |
| collaboration | the account by `Virality * Followers Coefficient * 50`, `happiness` by the `Engagement Score`, `karma` -1 when `Controversy Score` is 3 or more |
| hacked | `happiness` by the `Damage Score`, the account by `followers * Damage Score / 20` |

The collaboration's karma is the only karma the whole family can move. The hack is the
only branch that can take the account down, and it takes it down by a fraction: a
damage-5 hack on a twenty-thousand-subscriber account is a five-thousand-subscriber
year.

Every card also writes the family's ledger:

| line | written when |
| --- | --- |
| `I have N followers on <channel>.` | every card, in the channel's own term |
| `I have made N post(s) and been trolled N time(s)[, taken N sponsorship(s)][, filmed N collab(s)][, and been hacked N time(s)].` | every card |

### 91.4 The tokens

Three tokens had no resolver at all, and one of them is the reason the username family
had to be wired here.

| token | where the corpus uses it | what the port does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<username>` | 56 times, in exactly one file: troll-inbounds | generates a handle, pinned for the card |
| `<channel>` | 265 times over four files | reads `h.socialChannel` back |
| `<post>` | 15 times over two files, troll-inbounds and troll-outbounds | the channel's own `Post Type` word, lowercased, with post as the fallback |
| `<musician>` | the hacks table and one post type | already resolved by the music family |

`<channel>` and `<post>` are the two halves of one sentence shape: "Someone on
Instagram called rudecow960 replied to my post, saying I looked ugly." The channel is
part of the hero's life rather than of the event, so it is read back instead of drawn;
the noun is a property of the channel, because a tweet belongs to Twitter and a
livestream to Twitch.

The handle is the interesting one. A troll card names the same stranger twice - once in
the second-person `Scenario` and once in the first-person `Log Version` - and the
corpus has no column that could tie the two cells together. Drawing twice gives a card
whose body blames `the_denier9` while its own log blames `MathewsArianna`, which is
exactly what the first probe run printed. The year now draws the handle once, pins it
in `usernameOverride_` for the two resolves and clears it, and the sample cards below
show the two cells agreeing.

### 91.5 What it caught

1. **The cross-family residue detector earned its keep.** `spyres.py` reads every
   string of every event of a thirty-life run, not only its own family's rows, so this
   section's half-installed work surfaced inside a section 90 regression as
   `residue 74` - all of it `<post>` and the unresolved collaboration strings. It
   went back to zero once the two resolvers and the skip guard landed. It is the
   fastest way to see a half-installed family.
2. **The ledger line is not a good enough probe on its own.** The first check demanded
   that the post counter move on every card and reported 471 mismatches. A sponsorship,
   a collaboration and a hack leave the post and troll counters where they were; the
   probe now parses all five counters and asks only that none decrease and at least one
   move.
3. **A four-digit follower count looks like a mistake.** Read with the coefficients
   alone, a hero could post for twenty years and still show 150 followers, because the
   corpus's numbers are per-post ratios and no base. The x10 is the port's.
4. **The same stranger twice**: a real card-level bug, and one a residue check cannot
   see.
5. **"1 posts and been trolled 1 times."** The ledger counted with a fixed plural, and
   a life's first card is almost always a one.
6. **Two rows cannot be printed at all.** The hacks table and one post type name a
   `<musician>`, which the port can only resolve inside a music card; rather than
   print a bracket the year skips the row, the same shortcut section 90 took with its
   own two rows. It costs about one card in seventy.
7. **The probe had two bugs of its own**: the channel table was unpacked in the wrong
   order, so its rows came back as lists and the dictionary comprehension raised, and
   the ledger check above.

### 91.6 Shortcuts

- The year fires on 25% of the ages at 13 and up; the corpus has no rate.
- The five weights, 12/8/6/5/4, are the port's.
- The x100 likes base, the x10 follower scale and the x50 of a collaboration are the
  port's. The coefficients are the corpus's.
- The sponsorship's and the collaboration's sentences are the port's prose, because
  those two tables carry no `Scenario`.
- A row whose own text still needs a token the port has no source for is skipped rather
  than printed with a bracket in it.
- `a16_social-media-troll-outbounds-enc`, 38 rows, is not wired: it needs a victim
  the hero does not have. `a16_social-media-channels-onlyfans-tip-responses-enc`, 7
  rows, is not wired either: it needs a tip the port has no event for.
- One card a year, and the account is a follower count and nothing else. The
  `Post Verb`, `Post Description Present`, `Post Description Past`,
  `Impacted by Looks` and `Impacted by Smarts` columns are read for their channel
  flags and otherwise unused.

### 91.7 Verification

The probe drives 160 lives - two passes of forty seeds, both genders, to age 80 -
selects the five social tables, and checks the row index, the followers line
against the real channel row (its name, its `Followers Term`, and that its
Friends window still contains the hero), the five ledger counters, the happiness
and karma bounds of each kind, and that the body and the log each match the head
and tail of the row they came from.

## 92. The school year: a field trip with a theme, a prom that happens once, and a party whose parents are always away

The `a16_backtoschool` family is the largest unwired block left with real card text: fourteen
files and 357 rows, none of them referenced by the port before this section. Ten of those files
are wired here (264 rows) as the four events that share one year of a schoolchild's life - a
field trip whose museum theme decides what the class does, a school dance that needs a theme and
a companion before it can produce a verdict, a prom that can only happen once in a life, and a
house party whose rowdiness the port picks and whose hookup sentence comes out of its own table.
The remaining four files are the sleepover invitation and its acceptance feedback; they are
deferred to the next section because they are a four-choice card rather than a feedback line.

### 92.1 The family

| file | rows | columns that matter |
|---|---|---|
| `a16_backtoschool-field-trip-location-enc` | 14 | Location, Theme, Hero Min Age, Hero Max Age |
| `a16_backtoschool-field-trip-color-enc` | 37 | String, Focus, Theme |
| `a16_backtoschool-school-dance-theme-enc` | 6 | the theme name |
| `a16_backtoschool-school-dance-event-feedback-enc` | 34 | String, Companion Type, Dance Theme, Hero Enjoyment Score, NPC Enjoyment Score (if applicable) |
| `a16_backtoschool-school-dance-rejection-color-enc` | 34 | String, Hurtfulness Score, Commonness Score |
| `a16_backtoschool-prom-win-color-enc` | 23 | String, Gave Speech, Commonness Score |
| `a16_backtoschool-prom-lose-color-enc` | 20 | String, Commonness Score |
| `a16_backtoschool-house-party-color-enc` | 30 | String, Log Version, Rowdiness Level, Commonness Score |
| `a16_backtoschool-house-party-hookup-enc` | 38 | String, Rowdiness Level |
| `a16_backtoschool-house-party-parental-absence-color-enc` | 28 | String, Commonness Score |

Four of these ten files are not card text at all, they are join keys. The field trip's location
carries a `Theme` (art, science, history, or blank on thirteen rows) and a Hero Min/Max Age
window of 6..17; its colour rows carry the same `Theme` column, so the museum the child visits
selects the pool of things that happen inside it. The dance's `Theme` column is a bare list of
six themes - TikTok Memes, Hoedown, Masquerade, Vampires vs. Werewolves, Decades, Euphoria - and
the feedback rows point back at it through `Dance Theme`, blank on some rows so that they fit
any theme. The party's `Rowdiness Level` is `chill`, `lively` or `wild`, ten rows each,
and the hookup table repeats the same three words in a column that is blank on seventeen of its
thirty-eight rows. `Companion Type` on the dance feedback is the counterpart of the same idea:
`none`, `friend`, `lover`, or a list of two.

The pools are small enough to quote. The field trip's Focus column splits the 37 colour rows into
goofing off (16), learning (12) and socializing (9); the dance's Companion Type splits 34 rows
into blank (7), none (9), `friend,lover` (8), `lover` (6) and three smaller spellings of the
same pair; the party's forty-eight party-and-hookup rows are the three levels with a blank group
in the middle. The prom is the only event with no theme at all: it is a win table and a lose
table, and fifteen of the twenty-three win rows carry the `Gave Speech` flag.

### 92.2 The four events

One card a year, drawn by availability rather than by a ladder - the lesson of section 87 is that
a branch whose pool is empty must not be able to poison the window of a later branch, so the year
is a weighted draw over the branches that can actually fire:

| branch | weight | when it can fire |
|---|---|---|
| a field trip | 8 | age 6..18, a location with a theme inside its age window, a colour row matching it |
| a school dance | 8 | age 14..18 |
| the prom | 12 | age 16..18 and never before in this life |
| a house party | 6 | age 14..18 |

The prom carries the largest weight because it can fire exactly once in a life: a card that is
available every other year of school must not crowd out the one that is not. The four results:

- **The field trip.** The location is drawn from the rows whose age window contains the child and
  whose `Theme` is not blank; the colour row is then drawn from the rows whose `Theme` matches
  or is blank. `Focus` decides the effects: learning adds 2 smarts and 1 happiness, socializing
  3 happiness and 1 relationship, goofing off 4 happiness and loses 2 discipline. The ledger line
  counts trips: `That was field trip number N to X.`
- **The school dance.** A theme is drawn from the six. The companion is the lover when there is
  one, and otherwise the classmate the port already keeps (`schoolClassmate`, drawn once and
  remembered). The refusal branch fires when the lover's relationship is below 45 or on a 20%
  coin: the rejection rows are drawn by `Commonness Score` and their `Hurtfulness Score` (1..5)
  is subtracted from happiness - and from the relationship as well, but only when the person
  doing the refusing is the lover. The acceptance branch draws a feedback row whose `Dance
  Theme` is blank or the drawn theme and whose `Companion Type` fits the companion: `lover`
  or `friend,lover` for a partner, `friend` or `none` for a classmate. The row's `Hero
  Enjoyment Score` moves happiness and its `NPC Enjoyment Score` moves the relationship, the
  latter only for a partner. A row whose Companion Type is `none` means the child went alone,
  and the log says so.
- **The prom.** One attempt a life, at 16 or later. The vote is won when looks are at least 60 or
  on a 25% coin; a win draws from the win table (8 happiness, 2 looks, and 2 more when the row is
  one of the fifteen that carry `Gave Speech`) and a loss from the lose table (4 happiness).
  The title follows the hero's gender: `Prom king` or `Prom queen`.
- **The house party.** The parents' absence is drawn first, by `Commonness Score`, from the
  table of reasons (a convention, a reunion, a relative, a medical trip abroad). Then the port
  rolls the rowdiness itself - `chill` below 0.40, `lively` below 0.75, `wild` above, because
  the corpus ships the three levels in equal numbers and no score to choose between them - and
  draws a colour row of that level or a blank one. `chill` adds 3 happiness, `lively` 4 and 1
  discipline, `wild` 5 happiness, 3 discipline and 1 karma. A 45% coin then hooks the child up
  with the lover or with the same classmate, drawing a hookup row of the same level and appending
  its sentence to the party. The ledger counts parties: `I have hosted N house parties.`

### 92.3 The tokens

This family needed no new resolver, which is worth stating because three of the last four
sections did. Every token its 306 string rows use - `<classmate>`, `<celebrity>`,
`<musician-indefinite>`, `<city>`, `<country-possessive>`, `<hero-first-name>`,
`<drug-illegal>`, the numbered `<numA-B>` forms - is already handled. `<song>` and
`<movie>` look like tokens but are not: they are the stems of inline slash lists that the
generic list resolver eats. The one thing the section had to add is a guard: a row whose text
still holds a bracket after resolution is skipped rather than printed, which is the same shortcut
sections 90 and 91 took for the handful of rows that name a thing the port has no pool for.

### 92.4 What it caught

1. **Placement was worth more than the weights.** The family was first called from the end of the
   year chain, next to the social media year, where roughly fifty other families had already had
   their chance; two hundred lives produced a card or two. It now runs immediately after the
   school family (`src/sim.cpp:3401`, just below `schoolYear` at `src/sim.cpp:3400`), where
   the year is still young and the child's own school life has priority.
2. **A text search needs a scope.** The first patch searched for the branch marker `} else if
   (kind == 1) {` and found the wrong family: that string occurs fourteen times in `src/sim.cpp`,
   and the patch clobbered a branch belonging to somebody else. The recovery was to throw the file
   away (`git checkout -- src/sim.cpp`) and re-apply every edit with the search anchored at
   `s.index('bool Sim::backToSchoolYear')` and an assertion that the replaced range contains no
   other function definition.
3. **The corpus writes a sentence that starts with a pronoun token.** Rows such as `<he/she>
   told you that you were the best kisser...` resolve to a lowercase `she` in the port. The
   field trip, dance and hookup bodies now go through the capitalising helper, so the card reads
   `She told you...`.
4. **A trailing space hides the full stop.** Several rows end `...talking about it. `, and the
   tail's last-character test sees the space, not the period, and appends another one, which is
   how a card ends `It. .`. The tail now trims trailing whitespace before the test.
5. **The party had no title.** Its three levels produce the card body, but the row belongs to a
   colour table with no title of its own, so the card fell back to the year's default. It now
   reads `A house party`, and the four events have four titles.
6. **The prom needed a wider window.** At 17..18 the prom produced two cards in two hundred
   lives, because it has to win a weighted draw against every other family in the same year.
   Opening it at 16 is the port's own choice and is what makes the event visible at all.
7. **One corpus row is missing an article and it is not the port's fault.** The parents' absence
   table can produce `My parents went to visit theme park, so I hosted a house party.` - the
   inline list on that row offers bare nouns where the rest of the table offers `an` phrases.
   The card is left exactly as the corpus wrote it.

### 92.5 Shortcuts

1. The family fires on 30% of the school years for which it is eligible. It ships no gate column;
   the rate is the port's own, chosen so the four events are visible without owning the year.
2. The four weights (8, 8, 12, 6) are the port's own. The prom's 12 exists only because it can
   fire once a life.
3. The party's rowdiness roll (0.40 / 0.75) is the port's own; the corpus ships three equally
   common levels and no score to rank them by.
4. Every colour pool is drawn with `weightedPick` on `Commonness Score`, which falls back to
   a uniform draw when a table has no such column.
5. The dance's other half is the classmate the port already keeps; the corpus's `Child`,
   `Son` and `Daughter` audiences and its friend list do not exist in the port, so a stranger
   of the right gender stands in.
6. The prom's win condition (looks at least 60, or a 25% coin) and the dance's refusal condition
   (a relationship below 45, or a 20% coin) are both the port's own; the corpus supplies the
   result tables and nothing that decides between them.
7. The four sleepover files (93 rows) are not wired: their invitation is a four-choice card with
   its own narrative and four impact columns per choice, which is a section of its own.
8. One card a year, like every other family in this port.

narrative second, which is the same order every other family uses.
